add_nodes.title: Megawatt-class compute satellites fly
add_nodes.description: A compute satellite with at least 1 MW of solar power flies and operates. That is four times the 250 kW Starmind design, with roughly 4,000-6,000 m2 of array and a high-voltage power bus.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Starmind's design point rose from 150 kW peak (Jun 2026) to 250 kW peak and 175 kW average (Aug 2026); SpaceX's Sep 16 2026 FCC response bounds it under 4,000 kg, 200 m2 of radiator and 1,500 m2 of solar. Starcloud-3 (~200 kW) is designed for Starship. 33FG estimates that holding a 256-expert model inside one 72-GPU satellite costs up to 44% of serving output (Jul 2026). No flight-dated compute satellite above about 250 kW was found as of Oct 2026.
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: Not an AI-math implication in its timing: satellite size is a SpaceX design choice on the hardware clock, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. Cheap launch removes the reason to keep satellites small, and a larger satellite holds more GPUs inside one coherent domain, which cuts the penalty of splitting a model across satellites (up to 44% of serving output for one 72-GPU satellite, 33FG). At 1 MW a 250 V bus would carry 4,000 A, so the design pulls in 300-800 V buses (materials-wbg-rad-hard-power, struct-hv-power-bus-stability) and 4,000-6,000 m2 deployable arrays whose shape and loads must be predicted (struct-deployment-mechanics). These are the AI-math inputs, all soft. Chain (S2): first Starmind flights 2028 -> yearly generations from 2030 -> a MW-class design after two generations of telemetry, qualified and flown in 2032. S3 is a year earlier through faster generations. Bands (judgment): Medium by 2035 in S2-S4 because SpaceX may prefer many 250 kW satellites in tight formation; S1 Low.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: SpaceX may keep satellites near 250 kW and scale by numbers and formation flying, as Starlink did. Software that shrinks the single-satellite penalty would remove the main reason to go bigger.
add_nodes.signpost: A Starmind version or competing design above 500 kW announced with a flight date; a SiC or GaN power stage above 300 V named on a compute satellite.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. S4 equals S3 because the S3 year is 2031, before robots count, and the gates are qualification of large deployables and power electronics.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-orbital-compute-power (2026-10-07): new node extending the hardware chain past the first 100-kW-class flights; gives the deployment, bus-stability and SiC nodes a 2032-35 outcome.

revisions.reason: 2035 extension: new node

add_nodes.title: 10 GW of compute operating in orbit
add_nodes.description: Orbital data centers with at least 10 GW of combined power operate in orbit, about 40,000 satellites at 250 kW or fewer larger ones.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Orbital compute is at kilowatt scale. Musk has suggested Starship could support about 10 GW a year of space compute in the 2030s and projected 300-500 GW a year later (Nov 2025). Beijing Astro-Future has proposed 16 GW of dawn-dusk orbital data centers. Anthropic and SpaceX said in May 2026 that they are interested in jointly developing multiple GW of orbital compute. Approved Starship site caps total about 145 launches a year (Starbase 25, LC-39A 44, SLC-37 76).
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous anchor on launch, satellite production, chip supply and capital, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. At 16,000-18,000 t per GW today, or about 10,000 t at 100 kW/t, 10 GW is 100,000-180,000 t: about 700-1,800 Starship flights at 100-150 t, or five to twelve years of today's approved site caps. Chain (S2): 1 GW in 2031-32 -> 300+ heavy flights a year from 2033 (capability-35-heavy-cadence-300) -> compute takes a third to a half of them -> 2-3 GW a year by 2034-35 -> 10 GW cumulative in 2035, with no slack. S3 is a year earlier because heavy cadence and compute demand arrive earlier. Capital is large but reachable: Mach33's base case puts orbital capex at $46B per GW, falling toward $24B over a decade, so 10 GW is roughly $240-460B (a single commercial forecaster's model). Musk names chip and packaging supply as the main limit. AI math is second-order: hotter chips, lighter radiators and right-sized radiation mitigation cut launched mass by a few percent to about 10%. S4 gets no credit: robots speed satellite and array lines, but those already run ahead of flights, and pads and approvals do not compress. Bands (judgment): S2 Low because the chain has no slack; S3 and S4 Medium; S1 Speculative because a plateau weakens compute demand.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: AI mathematics could vanish from the chain without moving this node by more than months: launch cadence, chip supply and capital set the date. If terrestrial power and permits ease, orbital compute may stall well below 10 GW.
add_nodes.signpost: Starmind production above 10,000 satellites a year, or more than 150 dedicated compute flights in one year, by 2033; SpaceX reporting several GW deployed by end-2033.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. S4 adds nothing because launch binds; robots speed satellite and array lines that already run ahead of flights.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-orbital-compute-power (2026-10-07): new node extending the spine past struct-gw-orbital-compute.

add_nodes.title: A large AI model is trained in orbit
add_nodes.description: An AI lab releases or deploys a model whose main training run, at least 1e26 FLOP, ran mainly on orbital compute.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Starcloud trained a small language model on one H100 in orbit within 38 days of its Nov 2025 launch. Anthropic and SpaceX said in May 2026 that they are interested in multiple GW of orbital compute, citing ground constraints on training and inference. 33FG argues that high orbits suit asynchronous training and low orbits suit inference (Dec 2025). No multi-satellite training run has been reported.
add_nodes.why: Training uses the most power and tolerates latency, so it is the workload that fits orbit best, and Anthropic named it among its reasons. It is also where radiation errors cost most: a silent error can corrupt weeks of work. That is where validated error rates (materials-see-system-models) and proven fault-tolerance bounds (materials-verified-fault-tolerance) earn their keep. A 1e26 FLOP run needs on the order of 100 NVL72-class satellites for about a month (calculation at about 40% utilization, assumption), so it spans several ten-satellite clusters (struct-formation-compute-clusters) joined by laser links and low-communication training methods. Chain (S2): paying operations 2029 -> clusters 2029-30 -> hundreds of MW in orbit 2031-32 -> a disclosed main run in 2033. S3 is a year earlier. Bands (judgment): Medium by 2035 in S2-S4 because ground sites may stay cheaper for the largest runs and labs may not say where a model trained; S1 Low.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Labs may keep their largest runs on the ground, where interconnect is denser and failed parts are easy to swap, and use orbit for inference. Even then AI mathematics moves the date by months, since fleet size and links bind.
add_nodes.signpost: A lab states that a released model's main training run ran in orbit; a training job spanning 50 or more compute satellites reported by 2032.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. S4 equals S3 because fleet size, optical links and labs' choices bind, and none of them is robot labor.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-orbital-compute-power (2026-10-07): new node giving the radiation side lane (error models -> proven fault tolerance) a 2032-35 outcome.

revisions.reason: 2035 extension: new node

add_nodes.title: Orbital compute at scale beyond dawn-dusk orbits
add_nodes.description: At least 100 MW of compute operates in orbits with eclipses or harsher radiation than dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, such as inclined low orbits, medium Earth orbit or high Earth orbit.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Starmind, Starcloud and Suncatcher designs use dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, which gives near-continuous sunlight, needs only ~100 um of coverglass and keeps array loss under 1% a year (33FG, Dec 2025). 33FG estimates the dawn-dusk band is about 1% of usable low-orbit volume; in medium Earth orbit, belt exposure drives coverglass to ~700 um and array loss to ~3% a year.
add_nodes.why: Dawn-dusk orbits give near-continuous sun and mild radiation, so early fleets stay there and leave only when the band fills. At 10 GW, about 40,000 satellites at 250 kW, slot allocation, conjunction risk and licensing start to push fleets elsewhere. Inclined low orbits put batteries through about 5,500 eclipse cycles a year; higher orbits raise array loss from under 1% to about 3% a year and raise chip error rates. Here the branch's AI-math side lanes pay off: validated workload-level error rates (materials-see-system-models), proven fault-tolerance bounds (materials-verified-fault-tolerance) and model-based battery qualification (materials-battery-life-qual) let operators size shielding, batteries and mitigation before flight data exist. Chain (S2): dawn-dusk fleets reach several GW in 2033 -> a first non-dawn-dusk tranche authorized and flown in 2034. Bands (judgment): Low by 2035 in S2-S4 because MW-class satellites let dawn-dusk shells hold 10 GW or more and the chain needs fleets near 10 GW; S1 Speculative.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Larger satellites let dawn-dusk shells hold well over 10 GW, and operators may fly, measure and iterate in a new orbit instead of relying on models; AI mathematics then changes little.
add_nodes.signpost: An FCC or ITU filing for compute satellites in inclined low, medium or high Earth orbit; published error and degradation statistics from a compute satellite outside dawn-dusk orbit.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. S4 equals S3 because licensing, launch and the cost of batteries and shielding bind.
add_nodes.revision_note: E-orbital-compute-power (2026-10-07): new node giving the radiation and battery lanes a 2033-35 outcome.

patch.thesis: SpaceX's launch, hardware and capital clock paces orbital compute. Base case: 100-kW-class satellites fly about 2028, 1 GW is Low by 2031 and High by 2035, 10 GW Low by 2035. AI math adds a few percent; arrays and chip temperatures matter more. Robots (S4) change little: launch binds.
patch.reader_hook: A gigawatt of orbital compute is about 4,000 Starmind-class satellites and 110-180 Starship flights. Ten gigawatts needs about 700-1,800 flights, five to twelve years of today's approved Starship launch caps (about 145 a year). Qualifying chips to run about 30 C hotter saves about 1,900 t per GW (33FG model); AI radiator design might save 350-1,400 t (an assumption).
patch.revision_note: B-orbital-compute-power resolver (2026-10-07): Thesis rewritten so AI math is no longer stated as the condition for orbital compute (all three lenses); 1 GW band per the resolved node (S2 Low, S3 Medium). Reader hook re-based on the Sep 2026 filing envelope and 33FG's Oct 6 2026 model, flags the 10-25% as an assumption (auditor), and names the solar and chip-temperature levers (skeptic, advocate, auditor). Spine re-cut (skeptic: the old spine jumped between unconnected nodes): it now renders the physical anchor tree (100-kW radiator flight -> commercial operations -> 1 GW, with arrays, hot-chip qualification and 100 kW/t) beside the AI-math side chains (fault models -> proven fault tolerance; AI radiator design). cap-physics-theory added to roots (soft edge to SiC power). | C-fix (2026-10-07): spine rebuilt so it forms one connected chain of hard edges that reaches tier 6-7. Moved from spine to side_chains (still branch members): ['materials-see-system-models', 'materials-verified-fault-tolerance', 'struct-radiator-optimization']. The main chain is hardware on SpaceX's clock, matching the thesis; the AI-math lanes (radiation models, radiator optimization) feed it only softly. | E-orbital-compute-power (2026-10-07): thesis extended to 2035 and S4 (1 GW High by 2035 in S2-S4; 10 GW Low in S2, Medium in S3-S4; robots add one year only to the kilometre-scale structure). Reader hook re-based on the 10 GW launch count against today's approved Starship caps. Spine extended to struct-35-10gw-orbital-compute; three side lanes added for the new MW-class, training-run and beyond-dawn-dusk nodes.
